newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico almost completes debt refinancing for year.
newsitem.headline: Mexico almost completes debt refinancing for year.

text.p: Mexico has almost completed refinancing its debt issues for 1996 and hopes to extend the maturities of its debt coming due in 1997, Finance Ministry Director of Public Credit Martin Werner told financial analysts in New York on Wednesday.
Werner said there is $1.5 billion worth of paper maturing in November, but that the government has successfully covered 90 percent of the maturing paper.
It recently placed an eight-year 1.0 billion D-mark bond issue.
On Wednesday Mexico also launched a 70 billion yen samurai bond due September 30, 2002. The bond carries a coupon rate of 5.0 percent and were priced at par, lead manager Daiwa Securities said.
"We have almost completed our refinancing in the markets for 1996," Werner said.

Of the Mexican government or state corporation debt coming due in 1997, $5.0 billion is non-market debt owed under bilateral or multilateral arrangements, and about $4.0 billion will be refinanced in capital markets.

Of that total, $100 million is for the electric company, $800 million for oil company Pemex, $800 million for state development bank Nafin, $900 million for export development bank Bancomext and $1.4 billion for the federal government.
"We would like to extend the tenor of the United Mexican States debt, hopefully with medium and long-term issues," Werner said.
Mexico's external debt was about $98 billion at end of June compared to about $100 billion at the end of last year.
The $2.4 billion decrease was due to net amortizations and currency effects, Werner said.
About 30 percent of the external debt is non-dollar denominated.
Internal debt at the end of June was 163 billion pesos, compared with 155 billion at the end of last year.
The net public debt to GDP ratio declined to 32.6 percent at the end of June compared with 38.9 percent at the end of December last year, he said.
External debt makes up 27.3 percent of that, while domestic debt makes up 5.3 percent, he added.
Werner said that Mexico will have to make payments worth $3.3 billion to the International Monetary Fund in 1998 and $6.0 billion in 1999.
He said that the Mexican government could pay back what it owes from reserves, by financing by the federal government in capital markets or by negotiating an extension to the debt.
